card.name: Kachchhi Ghodi dance
card.tagline: Rajasthani mock-horse dancers wield swords to recount tales of legendary bandits.
card.profile: Originating in the Shekhawati region of Rajasthan, the Kachchhi Ghodi dance is a vivid folk tradition executed by male dancers fitted with elaborately decorated dummy horse costumes around their waists. Accompanied by dhol drums and flutes, performers enact mock fights while singers narrate tales of local bandits such as Bhanwariya. The dance is prominently featured during wedding processions to welcome the groom's party as well as in other social celebrations across India.
card.insight: In the Shekhawati region of Rajasthan, male dancers step into legless papier-mâché horse frames and clash swords in fast formations resembling opening flowers.
card.profile_long:
The Kachchhi Ghodi dance emerged from the Shekhawati region of Rajasthan, situated in western India, where it has long been performed by communities such as the Kamdholi, Sarghara, Bhambi, and Bhavi. Over time, the tradition extended beyond its regional roots to be adopted across India, including in Maharashtra and Gujarat. The dance centers around male performers who don elaborate mock-horse frames, stepping inside lightweight structures to simulate riding on horseback during festive gatherings, social celebrations, and wedding ceremonies to entertain and welcome the bridegroom's party.

Technically, the performance combines physical agility with precise group movement. Dancers wearing ghungroo (ankle bells) run back and forth while brandishing swords. When multiple dancers execute these rapid linear passes across from one another, their intersecting lines create an illusion that, when viewed from above, resembles the opening and closing of a flower. The dancers move to the rhythm of dhol drums and flute music, coordinating their steps with the percussive tempo.

The music and narrative elements of Kachchhi Ghodi are deeply tied to local lore. As the dancers engage in mock sword battles, singers deliver live vocal narrations detailing the exploits of local bandits, such as Bhanwariya, a figure regarded in Rajasthani folklore as an equivalent to Robin Hood. The soundscape combines the deep boom of the dhol, melodic lines of the flute, percussive accentuation from the dancers' ghungroo, and dramatic vocal storytelling.

The costume is a distinctive focal point of the art form. The dancer wears a traditional kurta and turban, with the horse's upper body shell constructed from papier-mâché molded over a flexible bamboo frame. This shell is covered in bright fabric decorated with intricate Shisha mirror-work embroidery. Because the dummy horse has no legs of its own, flowing fabric drapes down from the dancer's waist, concealing their legs to maintain the visual illusion of a mounted rider.

While predominantly performed during secular celebrations such as weddings and cultural festivals, similar horse-costume dances exist in other parts of India, such as the Poikkal kuthirai aattam of Tamil Nadu, which features wooden stilts to mimic hoofbeats during temple festivals. For professional Kachchhi Ghodi dancers, the tradition represents both an artistic livelihood and a vibrant preservation of Rajasthani folklore.

sections.origins_and_history: The Kachchhi Ghodi dance originated in the Shekhawati region of Rajasthan, India. It is traditionally associated with and performed by members of the Kamdholi, Sarghara, Bhambi, and Bhavi communities. Over time, its popularity spread beyond Rajasthan, becoming an adopted folk tradition in other Indian states, including Maharashtra and Gujarat.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performers step inside a novelty horse frame secured around the waist and move across the performance space. In group formations, dancers stand on opposite sides holding swords and run back and forth quickly. When viewed from above, this rapid back-and-forth movement creates the visual illusion of flowers opening and closing. Dancers keep time with ankle bells (ghungroo) to the beat of dhol drums and flute music.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is performed to the accompaniment of musicians playing the dhol (drum) and flute. A live singer narrates folk tales of mock fights, focusing on the exploits of local bandits such as Bhanwariya, considered the Rajasthani equivalent of Robin Hood. The dancers' ankle bells (ghungroo) add rhythm to every step.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear a traditional kurta and turban. The novelty horse costume features a papier-mâché shell built over a bamboo frame, embellished with brightly colored fabric and Shisha (mirror-work embroidery). The dummy horse does not have legs; instead, fabric drapes from the dancer's waist to cover the legs entirely. Ghungroo bells are tied around the ankles. It is typically performed in open settings, streets during wedding processions, or stage shows.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Kachchhi Ghodi is commonly performed during wedding ceremonies to welcome and entertain the bridegroom's party, as well as during diverse social settings and cultural events. For some dancers, performing the art form serves as a professional livelihood. The narrative aspects celebrate local heroism and traditional folklore.
sections.regional_variants: While originating in the Shekhawati region of Rajasthan, the dance is performed under the same name in Maharashtra and Gujarat. In Tamil Nadu, a similar folk dance called Poikkal kuthirai aattam ('false-leg horse dance') is performed during annual Amman Temple festivals in Thanjavur using wooden legs to simulate hoofbeats.
sections.lineage: Historically rooted in the folk culture of Rajasthan's Shekhawati region, the dance forms part of the heritage of the Kamdholi, Sarghara, Bhambi, and Bhavi communities, evolving into a recognized Indian folk dance form.

basic_steps: Step into the horse costume frame and secure it at the waist.
Tie ghungroo (ankle bells) securely around both ankles.
Hold a sword in hand while maintaining upright posture inside the dummy horse frame.
Perform rapid back-and-forth linear runs directly facing another dancer to form intersecting flower-like patterns.
teaching.rhythm: Rhythmic percussive beats driven by the dhol and punctuated by ankle bells (ghungroo).
teaching.formation: Linear facing lines where opposing rows of dancers run back and forth.
teaching.level_notes: Requires coordination to maneuver inside a rigid costume frame while handling a prop sword.

claims.text: Kachchhi Ghodi dance originated in the Shekhawati region of Rajasthan.
Dancers wear novelty horse costumes and participate in mock fights while narration is sung.
The dance is commonly performed during wedding ceremonies to welcome the bridegroom's party.
The dummy horse costume shell is made of papier-mâché on a bamboo frame covered in mirror-work fabric.
Opposing dancers running back and forth with swords resemble opening and closing flowers from above.
The dance is prevalent among the Kamdholi, Sarghara, Bhambi, and Bhavi communities.
Kachchhi Ghodi is currently practiced as a living dance and profession for some individuals.
